name: Backend interview concepts
description: Terms that come up in backend and system design interviews, one short answer each.

words.translation: Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.
Under a network partition you keep either consistency or availability, not both.
Replicas disagree for a while, then converge if writes stop.
Write with a version check and retry on conflict, instead of holding a lock.
Take the lock first, so nobody else can touch the row while you work.
Atomic, consistent, isolated, durable — the guarantees of a database transaction.
How much a transaction may see of others still in flight.
Reading a row another transaction wrote and then rolled back.
The same query returns new rows because someone inserted between reads.
Prepare everywhere, then commit everywhere — one coordinator, and it can block.
A long transaction split into steps, each with a compensating undo.
Messages arrive, possibly more than once, so consumers must be idempotent.
Not achievable end to end; approximated by at-least-once plus deduplication.
A slow consumer telling a fast producer to slow down instead of dropping work.
Stop calling a failing dependency for a while, so it can recover.
Separate resource pools, so one saturated dependency cannot sink everything.
Everything retries or refills at the same moment and knocks the service over.
Retry after a random extra delay, so clients do not resynchronise.
One expired key sends every request to the origin at once.
Writes go to cache and store together, so the cache is never stale.
Writes hit the cache and reach the store later — fast, and lossy on a crash.
Deciding when a cached value stopped being true. Famously the hard part.
Splitting data across databases by a key, so no single one holds it all.
Key placement that moves only a small share of keys when a node joins or leaves.
One shard takes most of the traffic because the key is badly chosen.
A copy serving reads only, lagging the primary by some amount.
Requiring a majority to agree, so two conflicting decisions cannot both win.
Picking one node to make decisions, and noticing when it dies.
Two nodes both believe they are the leader and both accept writes.
The slowest 1% of requests. Averages hide it, and users feel it.
One request fans out to many, so it is as slow as the slowest of them.
The measurement, the target you hold yourself to, and the promise with consequences.
How much unreliability the SLO allows before feature work stops.
Two full environments; switch traffic over, switch back if it goes wrong.
Send a small share of traffic to the new version and watch before going on.
Ship the code switched off, turn it on separately from deploying.
One query for the list, then one per row — the classic ORM performance bug.
Every connection is checked out and waiting, so new work queues forever.
Delegated authorisation: an app acts for a user without learning their password.
A signed token carrying claims. Readable by anyone, revocable by nobody.
Another site makes the browser send an authenticated request you did not intend.
Input treated as query syntax. Fixed by parameters, never by escaping.
Grant the smallest access that lets the job be done, and no more.
Several independent controls, so one failure does not expose everything.
